observation.visible_scene: A person, visible only as forearms, hands and the edge of a dark torso/apron, works with several lumps of reddish-brown clay on a pale pink tabletop. The background (crumpled plastic sheeting and out-of-focus shelving) stays fixed, indicating a stationary camera; a faint reddish clay smear marks the spot where the hands work.
visible_changes: At the start both hands press and knead a single irregular clay lump at the left-centre of the table, fingers spreading and closing repeatedly (some frames show hand motion blur).
Through this rolling/pressing the lump is progressively deformed from a crumpled mass into a smooth spherical ball (clearly formed by around t=1.1 s); the hands then briefly hold and turn the ball.

The right arm then translates across the table toward the cluster of lumps on the right; the hand grabs and rolls one of them, and a second smooth ball appears at the right side (visible by ~t=2.5 s).
The hands return to the left-centre and resume pressing/kneading an irregular lump there through the end of the clip.
The remaining loose lumps in the right cluster stay roughly in place throughout; only the lump under the working hand changes shape.
All shape changes and positions of the clay are produced by the hands (deformation and translation), not by camera motion, since the background and table edge do not shift.
outside_clip_unknowns: What the rolled balls are eventually used for, and whether more clay is added or removed outside this window.
The exact start of the kneading (already underway at t=0) and the final outcome after t=3.2 s.
Whether the person is working one lump at a time in a fixed sequence or rearranging them off-camera.
uncertain_details: Material is identified as clay only from its colour and malleable appearance; not confirmed.
The precise number of distinct lumps on the right is hard to fix because they overlap and partly occlude one another.
Hand positions in blurred frames (e.g. t=0.24, 0.48, 0.80, 1.20, 2.16) make the exact grip/rolling pose uncertain.
Minor apparent shifts of the table edge may be due to body movement rather than camera motion; camera is treated as essentially static.
